paragraphs: He had slipped back into his earlier tone of resentful buffoonery. Alyosha felt, though, that the man trusted him. If someone else had been standing in Alyosha’s place, he thought, the captain would not have spoken so openly or told what he had just told. This encouraged Alyosha, whose heart was trembling on the edge of tears.
“Oh, how I would love to make friends with your boy!” he cried. “If you could arrange it—”
“Certainly, sir,” muttered the captain.

“But now listen to something quite different!” Alyosha went on. “I have a message for you. That same brother of mine, Dmitri, has insulted his fiancée too, a noble-hearted girl you have probably heard of. I have the right to tell you about the wrong done to her. In fact I ought to, because when she heard of the insult done to you, and learned all about your unfortunate situation, she asked me at once, just now, to bring you this help from her. It is from her alone, not from Dmitri, who has abandoned her. It is not from me, his brother, or from anyone else, but from her, only from her! She begs you to accept her help.... You have both been insulted by the same man. She thought of you only when she had just received a similar insult from him, similar in its cruelty, I mean. She comes like a sister to help a brother in misfortune.... She told me to persuade you to take these two hundred roubles from her, as from a sister, knowing how badly you need them. No one will know about it, and it can give rise to no unjust slander. Here are the two hundred roubles, and I swear you must take them, unless—unless all men on earth are to be enemies! But there are brothers even on earth.... You have a generous heart ... you must see that, you must,” and Alyosha held out two new, rainbow-colored hundred-rouble notes.

They were both standing by the great stone close to the fence, and there was no one near. The notes seemed to make a tremendous impression on the captain. He started, but at first only from astonishment. This was the last thing he had expected to come of their conversation. Nothing could have been further from his dreams than help from anyone, and such a sum!
He took the notes, and for a minute he was almost unable to answer. A completely new expression came into his face.
“That is for me? So much money, two hundred roubles! Good heavens! Why, I haven’t seen so much money in four years! Mercy on us! And she says she’s a sister.... And is that the truth?”
“I swear that everything I told you is the truth,” cried Alyosha.
The captain flushed red.

“Listen, my dear, listen. If I take it, I won’t be behaving like a scoundrel? In your eyes, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I won’t be a scoundrel? No, Alexey Fyodorovitch, listen, listen,” he hurried on, touching Alyosha with both his hands. “You’re persuading me to take it, saying a sister sends it, but inwardly, in your heart, won’t you despise me if I take it, eh?”
“No, no, I swear on my salvation I won’t! And no one will ever know except me, you and she, and one other lady, her great friend.”

“Never mind the lady! Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch, at a moment like this you must listen, because you can’t understand what these two hundred roubles mean to me now.” The poor fellow was rising little by little into a sort of incoherent, almost wild excitement. He was thrown off balance and talked extremely fast, as though afraid he would not be allowed to say all he had to say.

“Besides being honestly come by, from a ‘sister’ so highly respected and revered, do you know that now I can look after mamma and Nina, my hunchback angel of a daughter? Doctor Herzenstube came to us out of the kindness of his heart and examined them both for a whole hour. ‘I can make nothing of it,’ he said, but he prescribed a mineral water that is sold at the chemist’s here. He said it would be sure to do her good, and he ordered baths too, with some medicine in them. The mineral water costs thirty kopecks, and she’d need to drink forty bottles, perhaps. So I took the prescription and laid it on the shelf under the ikons, and there it lies. And he ordered hot baths for Nina, with something dissolved in them, morning and evening. But how can we carry out such a cure in our mansion, with no servants, no help, no bath and no water? Nina has rheumatism all over, I don’t think I told you that. Her whole right side aches at night, she is in agony, and would you believe it, the angel bears it without a groan, for fear of waking us. We eat what we can get, and she will only take the leavings, what you’d hardly give to a dog. ‘I’m not worth it, I’m taking it from you, I’m a burden on you,’ that is what her angel eyes try to say. We wait on her, but she doesn’t like it. ‘I’m a useless cripple, no good to anyone.’ As though she weren’t worth it, when she is the saving of all of us with her angelic sweetness! Without her, without her gentle word, it would be hell among us! She softens even Varvara. And don’t judge Varvara harshly either, she is an angel too, she too has suffered wrong. She came to us for the summer, and she brought sixteen roubles she had earned by giving lessons and saved up, to go back to Petersburg with in September, that is, now. But we took her money and lived on it, so now she has nothing to go back with. Though really she couldn’t go back anyway, because she has to work for us like a slave. She is like an overdriven horse with all of us on her back. She waits on us all, mends and washes, sweeps the floor, puts mamma to bed. And mamma is capricious and tearful and insane! And now, with this money, I can get a servant, you understand, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I can get medicines for the dear creatures, I can send my student to Petersburg, I can buy beef, I can feed them properly. Good Lord, it’s a dream!”
Alyosha was delighted that he had brought the man such happiness, and that the poor fellow had agreed to be made happy.

“Wait, Alexey Fyodorovitch, wait,” the captain went on with frenzied speed, carried away by a new daydream. “Do you know, Ilusha and I may really carry out our dream. We’ll buy a horse and cart, a black horse, he insists it must be black, and we’ll set off just as we pretended the other day. I have an old friend, a lawyer in K. province, and I heard through a trustworthy man that if I came he would give me a place as a clerk in his office. So, who knows, maybe he would. Then I’d just put mamma and Nina in the cart, and Ilusha could drive, and I’d walk, I’d walk.... Why, if I only manage to get one debt paid that’s owed me, I might have enough for that too!”

“There would be enough!” cried Alyosha. “Katerina Ivanovna will send you as much more as you need, and you know, I have money too. Take what you want, as you would from a brother, from a friend, and you can give it back later.... (You’ll get rich, you’ll get rich!) And you know, you couldn’t have a better idea than to move to another province! It would be the saving of you, especially of your boy. And you ought to go quickly, before the winter, before the cold. You must write to us when you’re there, and we will always be brothers.... No, it’s not a dream!”

Alyosha could have hugged him, he was so pleased. But when he glanced at the man, he stopped short. The captain was standing with his neck stretched out and his lips pushed forward, his face pale and frenzied. His lips were moving as though he were trying to say something. No sound came, but still his lips moved. It was uncanny.
“What is it?” asked Alyosha, startled.

“Alexey Fyodorovitch ... I ... you,” muttered the captain, faltering, looking at him with a strange, wild, fixed stare and an air of desperate resolution. At the same time there was a sort of grin on his lips. “I ... you, sir ... wouldn’t you like me to show you a little trick I know?” he murmured suddenly, in a firm, rapid whisper, his voice no longer faltering.
“What trick?”
“A pretty trick,” whispered the captain. His mouth was twisted to the left side, and his left eye was screwed up. He still stared at Alyosha.
“What is the matter? What trick?” Alyosha cried, thoroughly alarmed now.

“Why, look,” squealed the captain suddenly. He showed him the two notes, which he had been holding by one corner between thumb and forefinger all through the conversation, and he crumpled them up savagely and squeezed them tight in his right hand. “Do you see, do you see?” he shrieked, pale and furious. And suddenly flinging up his hand, he threw the crumpled notes onto the sand. “Do you see?” he shrieked again, pointing at them. “Look there!”
And in wild fury he began trampling them under his heel, gasping and exclaiming as he did so:
“That’s what I think of your money! That’s what I think of your money! That’s what I think of your money! That’s what I think of your money!”
Suddenly he darted back and drew himself up in front of Alyosha, and his whole figure expressed unutterable pride.

“Tell those who sent you that the wisp of tow does not sell his honor,” he cried, raising his arm in the air. Then he turned quickly and began to run. But he had not run five steps before he turned right around and kissed his hand to Alyosha. He ran another five paces and then turned around for the last time. This time his face was not twisted with laughter but quivering all over with tears. In a tearful, faltering, sobbing voice he cried:
“What would I say to my boy if I took money from you for our shame?”

And then he ran on without turning. Alyosha looked after him, inexpressibly grieved. Oh, he saw that until the very last moment the man had not known he would crumple up the notes and fling them away. The captain did not turn back. Alyosha knew he would not. He would not follow him or call him back, and he knew why. When the man was out of sight, Alyosha picked up the two notes. They were badly crushed and crumpled, and had been pressed into the sand, but they were undamaged and even rustled like new ones when Alyosha unfolded them and smoothed them out. After smoothing them out, he folded them up, put them in his pocket and went to Katerina Ivanovna to report on the success of her commission.
